question: When taking a periapical of a lower third molar, what is the solution to positioning the receptor far enough back in the mouth?
options: Use specially designed or adapted holders
Use a modified bisected angle technique
Build up the area with cotton wool rolls
Ask the patient to suck a lozenge
explanation: Specially designed or adapted holders are used to position the sensor/film at the back of the mouth for lower third molars.
extraWrong: Ask the patient to breathe deeply
Hold it with a rubber dam clamp
Use a shorter exposure time

question: How can the entire lower third molar, its surrounding tissues and the inferior canal be recorded when one image is not enough?
options: Take one occlusal view with the receptor flat in the mouth
Take two periapicals with two different tubehead positions
Take one bitewing with a longer exposure
Take a single oblique lateral view instead of the periapical
explanation: Two periapical views are taken with the receptor as far back as possible, using two different X-ray tubehead positions.
extraWrong: Take two bitewings using the same tubehead position
Take one periapical using a longer exposure time
Take one periapical with the receptor flat in the occlusal plane

question: For a patient with a strong gag reflex, asking them to concentrate on breathing deeply while the receptor is in the mouth can help.
explanation: Concentrating on breathing deeply is one of the solutions for patients with a strong gag reflex.

question: For a patient with a strong gag reflex, why might the image receptor be placed flat in the mouth in the occlusal plane?
options: So it does not touch the palate
So the tubehead can be angled downwards
So the patient can hold it with a finger
So the exposure time can be reduced
explanation: Placing the receptor flat in the occlusal plane stops it touching the palate, reducing gagging.
extraWrong: So the image is magnified
So the root canals can be separated
So the inferior canal is recorded

question: Which of the following is a recommended solution for a patient with a strong gag reflex?
options: Build up the area with cotton wool rolls
Use an oblique lateral radiograph
Suck a local anaesthetic lozenge first
Use different horizontal tubehead positions
explanation: Sucking a local anaesthetic lozenge before positioning the receptor is a solution for a strong gag reflex.
extraWrong: Increase the exposure time
Use a special endodontic holder
Place the receptor against the palate

question: When X-raying a patient with a strong gag reflex, positioning problems are greatest in the anterior incisor regions.
explanation: The problem is mainly in the upper and lower posterior molar regions.

question: In partially dentate patients, how can the deficiency be built up to help receptor placement?
options: With a bite-peg
With a rubber dam clamp
With an adapted holder
With cotton wool rolls
explanation: In partially dentate patients, the deficiency can be built up using cotton wool rolls.
extraWrong: With a local anaesthetic lozenge
With an endodontic holder
With a rubber dam sheet

question: Which of these is a reason receptor placement is difficult in edentulous patients?
options: Lack of height in the palate
Presence of rubber dam clamps
Multi-rooted teeth
Excessive lingual sulcus depth
explanation: Problems include lack of palatal height, loss of lingual sulcus depth, and rotation or displacement of the holder.
extraWrong: Presence of endodontic instruments
Overlapping contact points
Too much height in the palate

question: Intra-oral periapicals for edentulous patients can be taken using a modified bisected angle technique.
explanation: A modified bisected angle technique is one solution for edentulous patients.

question: During endodontics, how can the root canals of a multi-rooted tooth be identified and separated?
options: Take one radiograph with a longer exposure and a larger receptor
Take two or three radiographs with different vertical tubehead angulations
Take two or three radiographs with different horizontal tubehead positions
Take an oblique lateral radiograph of the affected side
explanation: At least two or even three radiographs are taken using different horizontal X-ray tubehead positions.
extraWrong: Take a single bitewing of the tooth
Take one periapical with the receptor flat in the mouth
Take a single occlusal view of the whole arch

question: During endodontics with rubber dam in place, which of these is a solution for placing and stabilising the receptor?
options: Place it flat in the occlusal plane
A simple holder held by the patient
Build up the area with cotton wool
Take an extra-oral oblique lateral
explanation: A simple phosphor plate/film packet holder, positioned parallel to the tooth and held by the patient, or a special endodontic holder, can be used.
extraWrong: Ask the patient to suck a lozenge
Ask the patient to breathe deeply
Take two views of the third molar

question: Panoramic tomographs are the recommended alternative extra-oral radiographs for small children who cannot co-operate with intra-oral radiography.
explanation: The listed alternative extra-oral radiographs for small children are oblique laterals.

question: Which approach is recommended for intra-oral radiography of small children?
options: Take two views with different horizontal tubehead positions
Build up the deficiency with cotton wool rolls first
Use a specially designed or adapted paralleling holder
Place the receptor flat and use a modified bisected angle
explanation: For small children the receptor is placed flat in the occlusal plane and a modified bisected angle technique is used.
extraWrong: Ask the child to suck a local anaesthetic lozenge
Take two or three views at different vertical angles
Use a special endodontic sensor holder

question: What makes placing and stabilising image receptors difficult during endodontic treatment?
options: Endodontic instruments, rubber dam and clamps in position
Lack of height in the palate
Loss of lingual sulcus depth
Small mouth size in a young patient
explanation: During endodontics, endodontic instruments, rubber dam and rubber dam clamps make it hard to place and stabilise receptors.
extraWrong: Rotation of the holder on an edentulous ridge
Poor co-operation from a young child
Missing teeth that need building up with cotton wool

question: Which two factors make ideal receptor placement difficult when X-raying small children?
options: Rubber dam and endodontic instruments
Size of mouth and co-operation
Lack of palatal height and lingual sulcus depth
Rotation and displacement of the holder
explanation: In small children, the size of the mouth and co-operation make ideal receptor placement difficult.
extraWrong: Multi-rooted teeth and curved canals
Dense bone and thick soft tissues
Gold crowns and amalgam fillings

question: Apart from a simple holder held by the patient, what can be used to position receptors during endodontics?
options: Cotton wool rolls to build up the area
A local anaesthetic lozenge
An oblique lateral extra-oral view
A special endodontic film or sensor holder
explanation: During endodontics, either a simple phosphor plate/film packet holder held by the patient or a special endodontic film or sensor holder can be used.
extraWrong: Two periapicals with different vertical angles
A protective thyroid shield
Deep breathing during the exposure

question: Rotation or displacement of the image receptor holder can make receptor placement difficult in edentulous patients.
explanation: Problems in edentulous patients include lack of palatal height, loss of lingual sulcus depth, and rotation or displacement of the receptor holder.

question: Why might it be difficult to place an intra-oral image receptor accurately in an edentulous patient?
options: Patient unable to bite on bitepeg
Dentures getting in way
Lack of height in palate
Glasses getting in way
explanation: Shallow palates, loss of depth in lingual sulcus or too few teeth to stabilise image receptor holder.

question: What technique would be used when taking an intra oral radiograph with partially dentate patients?
options: Take intra oral periapicals using modified bisected angle technique
Use cotton wool rolls to build up deficiency
explanation: In partially dentate patients, build up the deficiency using cotton wool rolls.

question: What technique would be used to help when taking an intra oral radiograph with edentulous patients?
options: Take intraoral periapicals using modified bisected angle technique
Use cotton wool rolls to build up deficiency
explanation: For edentulous patients, intra-oral periapicals are taken using a modified bisected angle technique; cotton wool rolls are used to build up the deficiency in partially dentate patients.

question: When might the superimposition of root canals in multi rooted teeth be a particular problem?
options: In partially edentulous patients
When taking periapical radiographs during endodontics
When trying to image partially erupted third molars
When patient has strong gag reflex
explanation: During endodontics, identifying and separating the root canals of multi-rooted teeth is a problem, so two or three radiographs are taken at different horizontal tubehead positions.
